title: Review and comparison of algorithms and software for mixed-integer derivative-free optimization
contribution: Review of bound-constrained mixed-integer DFO algorithms plus a benchmark of 13 solvers on 267 bound-constrained problems derived from MINLPLib 2, scored against BARON-certified optima: MISO and NOMAD lead, no solver dominates, and a small covering set of solvers solves 93% of the problems together.
problem_entry: Benchmark gap: earlier MIDFO comparisons used specific applications or small test sets, so the paper extends Rios & Sahinidis 2013 from continuous to mixed-integer problems and asks which solvers reach near-global solutions and how quality falls with size (p. 2); the field's immaturity is argued from dated citation counts (p. 7; Table 2, p. 9).
key_idea: Review followed by a benchmark with certified ground truth: admit every open or commercial code with reported experience on the class (p. 7), certify each optimum with BARON (p. 13), score near-optimality, best-among-solvers and starting-point improvement at default settings (p. 13), and conclude with a minimal covering set of solvers (pp. 19-21); the taxonomy is kept from 2013 (p. 2).
assumptions: Bound constraints with finite boxes (p. 3); integer neighbourhoods defined by the user; f continuously differentiable in the continuous variables for the stationarity definitions (p. 3); test problems are MINLPLib 2 models with constraints dropped, 79 continuous ones made integer, at most 500 variables, and missing bounds set to [-10,000, 10,000] (p. 13).
proof_devices: No theorems (n/a for proofs); Defs. 1-4 of local minimum, stationary point, strong stationary point and combined local minimum for mixed-integer problems (pp. 3-4)
Success test: within 1% or 0.01 of the certified optimum, whichever is larger (p. 13)
Moré-Wild starting-point improvement test with f_L set to the certified global optimum (pp. 18-19)
Minimal sufficient solver set, excluding any solver whose solved problems are a strict subset of another's (p. 20)
Scaled objective 1 - |f_L - f_solver|/(1e-10 + |f_L|), clipped at 0, to compare variance across scales (p. 21)
Efficiency read as a Pareto plot of evaluations against fraction solved (p. 23)
experiments: 13 solvers (versions in Table 3, p. 14) and 267 problems (176 pure-integer, 91 mixed-integer; 52/102/113 small/medium/large); 2500 evaluations, five shared uniform random starting points, default settings, Xeon W-2123 (p. 13); fraction solved by class and size (pp. 14-18), starting-point improvement (pp. 18-20), covering sets (p. 20), variance (pp. 20-22), evaluations and CPU time (pp. 22-26); no developer rounds and no hold-out set.
positioning: Sequel to his own 2013 study, whose taxonomy it adopts (p. 2); descriptive review of the Audet-Dennis/MADS, Liuzzi-Lucidi-Rinaldi, Newby-Ali and Porcelli-Toint lines and of surrogate and metaheuristic methods (pp. 4-6); the verdict is left to the benchmark.
writing: The abstract leads with counts and named winners (p. 1) and the paper ends on a portfolio verdict (p. 27); numbers disagree in places without acknowledgment: the 93% covering set has six solvers on p. 20 and five on p. 27; MISO solves 59% vs 54% of large problems (pp. 18, 20); DAKOTA/SOGA scores 40-42% vs 31% on pure-integer and 13% vs 16% on mixed-integer problems (pp. 15, 17); NOMAD is called best where the text shows ties (pp. 1, 16-17).
limits_future: Stated: existing solvers cannot solve large and pure-integer problems efficiently (p. 26); large-scale methods are needed and constrained problems are left to future work (p. 27). Unstated: the budget is not tied to an application, the algebraic tests are stripped of constraints and some sit in artificial boxes (p. 13), and there is no hold-out set.

method_links.note: Steps 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 carried out on a new class: all implementations with reported experience, BARON-certified optima, identical starting points and boxes, an explicit success test with median and best runs, an Online Supplement and data URL, and a minimal covering set of solvers with a stated scope.

No developer rounds and no structurally new hold-out in 2022 (default settings only), and the budget is a bare 2500 evaluations, not tied to an application. SKILL.md's say-do tick for the 2022 study holds for steps 1-3, 5 and 6 but not for step 4.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Show the search before the score
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Before the statistics, two 2-D problems (st_e36 with its constraints dropped, and a synthetic integer problem with a large domain) plot every evaluated point of all 13 solvers to show local vs global and pattern vs random search.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Benchmark sequel on the adjacent class
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The taxonomy and design of the 2013 continuous DFO study are carried over to the mixed-integer class.

transferable: Build a black-box test set with certified optima from an algebraic library: drop the constraints, remove the variables this makes redundant, impose integrality on continuous models, and certify each optimum with a deterministic global solver (p. 13).
Give all solvers the same random starting points from the box; run deterministic solvers that ignore the starts once and stochastic ones once per start; report median and best runs (pp. 13-14).
Count a run as a success when it is within 1% or 0.01 of the certified optimum, whichever is larger (p. 13).
Report a minimal covering set of solvers per problem class, leaving out solvers whose solved problems are a strict subset of another's (p. 20).
Report 'tot' and 'opt' evaluation counts next to CPU time, and say which one matters for cheap and which for expensive functions (pp. 22-25).
coauthors: Nikolaos Ploskas (first author; University of Western Macedonia)

quotes.text: We used the general-purpose global optimization solver BARON [70] to obtain the global solution of each problem.
Overall, existing algorithms in this field are complementary in their performance. They should be used collectively rather than individually.

title: Deterministic symbolic regression with derivative information: General methodology and application to equations of state
contribution: A big-M disjunctive MINLP for symbolic regression that adds auxiliary first- and second-derivative expression trees sharing the operator binaries, so that derivative data or sign constraints (such as thermodynamic consistency) can be imposed; shown on two toy problems and on Peng-Robinson alpha functions for argon and CO2 solved with BARON.
problem_entry: Fixed-form regression restricts the functional form, and deterministic symbolic regression is limited by the complexity of its search space (p. 1); derivative information is brought in to shrink the search and keep models physically meaningful (p. 3), driven by the consistency rules for alpha functions (p. 13) and by neural networks being too large for solvers (p. 12).
key_idea: Auxiliary expression trees, one per derivative order, share the main tree's operator binaries and apply the chain rule to its node values, so that constraints on f' and f'' can be posed (pp. 7-9); the Cozad-Sahinidis disjunctive big-M model and the Kim et al. tree constraints are kept (pp. 4-6), and same-variable redundancy cuts and a node-count penalty near zero are added (pp. 9-10).
assumptions: Fixed depth D with 2^D - 1 nodes (p. 4); fixed operator set (p. 14); bounds on node values give big-M constants by interval arithmetic, and a tolerance epsilon guards operator domains (p. 6); one predictor per auxiliary tree (pp. 7-8); sum-of-squared-errors loss (p. 5); derivative constraints only at the data points (p. 15); lambda near zero (p. 10).
proof_devices: Node disjunctions reformulated by big-M, with constants from interval arithmetic on node-value bounds (p. 6)
Forward-mode chain rule written as constraints: auxiliary derivative trees that share the operator binaries (pp. 7-9; Tables 3-4, pp. 31-32)
Constraints that shrink the search space, listed with their sources, including new same-variable cuts and two rewrites left unconstrained (p. 9; Table 5, p. 33)
Node-count penalty lambda*sum(y) as a tie-breaker (eq. 5, pp. 9-10)
experiments: BARON 21.3.26 on an i7-5600U (p. 10); toy 1 fits two points with a line in 8.31 s, or with the quadratic in 45.63 s under sign constraints (Table 6, p. 34); toy 2 fits a saddle from 10 points plus 3 sign points in under 60 s (p. 11); case study fits Ar and CO2 alpha functions to NIST vapour pressure and liquid Cp at depths 3-5 with 1000 s runs passing cutoffs (p. 14); extrapolation failures are reported and a CO2 fit is refitted (pp. 15-16); Table 8 gives train/test errors without describing the split (p. 36); no optimality gaps and no baseline.
positioning: Set against genetic programming, Kaizen programming and AI Feynman (pp. 2-3); inside the deterministic line of Cozad et al., Neumann et al., Kim et al., Austel et al. and Wei and Yuan (p. 3); big-M form from Grossmann 2002 (p. 6); thermodynamics papers serve as the source of constraints (p. 13); no competing method is run.
writing: Novelty claimed in the abstract (p. 1); a candid weakness statement (p. 15) and the hedge 'further evaluation is required' (p. 10); constraints on variance are announced (p. 3) but never specified; the claim of overall adherence (p. 16) comes right after violations outside the data range are reported (p. 15).
limits_future: Stated: derivatives are constrained only at the data points, so extrapolation may break the physics (p. 15); a node penalty is needed for tractability (p. 14); future work: complexity control, constraints beyond the parent-children subtree, and the informational content of inputs and outputs (p. 16). Unstated: small depths, no optimality gaps, no comparison with other tools.

method_links.note: A motif basis seeded by physics, with a size penalty (steps 2-3); first-principles derivative constraints during fitting (step 4); points added where the fit violates the physics, then a refit (step 5); a physical reading of the selected terms (step 6); symbolic regression as a global MINLP solved with BARON (step 7).

Step 4's certification is not met: constraints hold only at sample points and the fits violate the physics outside the data range; the case-study runs are reported without gaps or termination status; the added points carry constraints only and need no new experiment, unlike error-maximization sampling.

Reduction of the search space moves into the model (redundancy and symmetry cuts, derivative information as a reducer, interval-arithmetic big-M), and incumbent cutoffs are passed between restarts to fathom worse solutions; range reduction at the nodes is not discussed.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Derivative-sign constraints at extra inputs replace measurements; points added where the fit violates the physics carry no output value and stay out of the sum of squared errors.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Time-sliced global solve with incumbent cutoff
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: BARON runs in 1000 s slices, each passing its improved upper bound to the next as a cutoff, then one 100,000 s run once a slice stops improving.

transferable: Encode each derivative order as an auxiliary expression tree that shares the main tree's operator binaries; the derivative rule for each operator becomes a table entry (Tables 3-4, pp. 31-32).
Impose qualitative physics, such as derivative signs, at extra points instead of measuring more data (pp. 10-11).
Where the fitted model breaks a physical rule, add constraint-only points and refit (p. 15).
In expression-tree MINLPs, cut trivial operations on the same variable: x - x, x/x, x + x and x*x (p. 9).
Compute big-M constants by interval arithmetic from bounds on the node values (p. 6).
Run a global solver in fixed time slices, passing each incumbent to the next as a cutoff, then finish with one long run (p. 14).
coauthors: Marissa R. Engle (first author; Carnegie Mellon, Department of Chemical Engineering)

quotes.text: Enforcing gradient conditions replaces the need for additional measurements and results in an accurate model.
This highlights a weakness of our current symbolic regression formulation in that it only addresses derivatives at the data points.

title: SDP-quality bounds via convex quadratic relaxations for global optimization of mixed-integer quadratic programs
contribution: Convex QCP relaxations for nonconvex MIQPs with linear equalities, built from possibly nonconvex quadratic cuts from nonuniform diagonal perturbations and separated by a regularized log-det coordinate method; they outer-approximate a semi-infinite program proven to lie between two SDP bounds and to equal the stronger one under a Slater condition. Implemented in BARON 20.4, they cut the shifted-geometric-mean CPU time by 29.6% on 259 solved instances and gaps by 25.7% on 863 unsolved ones.
problem_entry: Branch-and-bound efficiency depends on both the tightness and the cost of relaxations (p. 1); their own spectral relaxations were cheap and tight, SDP projections are tight but expensive to separate, and Dong's semi-infinite view is the starting point (p. 2).
key_idea: Cuts v >= x'(Q+diag(d))x - d'y, with d making Q+diag(d)+alpha*A'A PSD, are nonconvex but convex on Ax=b (Prop. 1, p. 4); alpha is used only in the separation problem (p. 12); a smooth, adaptive rho*d'd regularizer replaces Dong's fixed one (pp. 14, 17); inside BARON, the QCP loop runs only at the root, node QPs inherit perturbations, answers are checked against KKT, relaxations are selected dynamically, and the QPs stay off unless the root bound beats LP (pp. 18-19).
assumptions: A has full row rank (p. 3); Theorem 1 needs a strictly feasible nullspace SDP (p. 8); the sufficient conditions of Prop. 5 fail for binary variables (pp. 9-10), so the equivalence does not cover binary instances such as the CBQP library (p. 20); general integers get only an outer approximation (p. 19); the relaxations apply only to models of form (1) (p. 18).
proof_devices: Convexity by projection onto the nullspace of A (Prop. 1, pp. 4-5)
Monotonicity in alpha by inclusion of the perturbation sets, with alpha -> infinity tightest (Prop. 2, pp. 5-6)
Sandwich muSDPd <= muSICPda <= muSDPda from the self-duality of the PSD cone (Prop. 3, pp. 6-7)
Feasible X = xx' + ZWZ' by eigendecomposition (Prop. 4, pp. 7-8)
Equivalence by rewriting an SDP without a Slater point in nullspace coordinates, where Slater can hold, then strong duality (Theorem 1, pp. 7-9; Prop. 5 constructs a strictly feasible point, p. 9)
Best among the SDPs that lift valid quadratic equalities of Ax=b (Props. 6-7, Theorem 2, pp. 10-11)
Non-attainment counterexample with a dual explanation (Example 1, p. 14); attainment under rho*d'd via a strictly feasible primal-dual pair (Prop. 8, p. 15)
Closed-form coordinate step with a Sherman-Morrison update (Prop. 9, eqs. 47-51, pp. 15-16)
experiments: GAMS 30.1.0, Xeon X5650, one thread, 1e-6 tolerances, 500 s; 960 CBQP, 30 QSAP, 246 BoxQP and 315 EIQP instances from the authors' library (p. 20); root-gap profiles against Dong's separation per library, bounds only (pp. 20-22); BARON vs BARONnoqc on 1122 filtered instances, 259 solved (time, nodes, memory) and 863 unsolved (gaps), shifted geometric means down 29.6/57.7/47.7/25.7%, pooled across libraries, with losses on easy instances (pp. 21-23); per-library profiles against six solvers, and one-to-one runs against CPLEX and GUROBI with optimalitytarget 3 and nonconvex 2 (pp. 20, 24-25).
positioning: Partially inspired by Dong 2016, refines it and then beats his separation head-to-head (pp. 2, 20-22); Saxena-Bonami-Lee credited for tightness and criticized for cost (p. 2); BARON's portfolio cited through the group's own papers (p. 18); Faye-Roupin behind Theorem 2 (p. 10).
writing: Four numbered contributions (pp. 2-3); claims scoped 'for our test problems' (pp. 1, 25); 'significant' means outside a 10% band (pp. 22-23); the title's 'SDP-quality' rests on four selected-instance plots and root-gap profiles (pp. 20-22); the conclusion is a summary with no limits and no future work (p. 25).
limits_future: Stated in the body: the binary case falls outside Prop. 5 (p. 10), general integers get an outer approximation (p. 19), QCPs run only at the root because of cost (p. 19), and easy instances get slower (p. 22). Unstated: cost claims without timing data (pp. 16, 19), KKT rejections not counted, MaxNC and the parameter values unjustified (p. 17), no per-library ablation, and the authors' own libraries without a hold-out set; no future work (p. 25).

method_links.note: Cheap quadratic cuts approximate the SDP bound (step 3); the QCP runs only at the root because it costs an order of magnitude more than node QPs; dynamic relaxation selection (step 4); subsolver answers checked against KKT (step 5); QPs switched off when the root does not beat LP (step 6); ill-conditioning avoided; judged by time, with losses admitted.
Step 1 is not met at the level of the relaxation: the root-node study compares bounds only, without time or failure counts per relaxation; cost enters only through BARON's end-to-end CPU time.

Built into BARON 20.4 and judged against a like-for-like switch (BARONnoqc keeps the earlier spectral module); fixed protocol of GAMS, one thread, 1e-6 and 500 s; instances published as a library; baselines in their strongest fair mode (Heuristic 4).

Library-by-library reporting holds for the root-bound and solver profiles but not for the ablation itself (pooled in Figs. 3 and 5-6 and Table 1); the evaluation set is the authors' own library, with no hold-out.
Weak: node relaxations are built from unfixed variables only; variables fixed by Ax=b are eliminated before the theory applies; nodes that become convex get a plain continuous relaxation.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Prove where the cheap relaxation sits
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The semi-infinite relaxation that the cuts outer-approximate is sandwiched between two SDP bounds and equals the stronger one under Slater's condition, and that SDP is the best among SDPs that lift valid equalities.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Expensive once at the root, inherited below
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The QCP cutting surface runs only at the root; each node reuses its parent's perturbation (keeping bounds monotone) plus at most one new separation; d_root is the multiplier-weighted average of the root cuts; alpha is fixed at the root.
The separation infimum may not be attained (Example 1); a smooth rho*d'd regularizer guarantees attainment (Prop. 8); rho is raised, with a restart, when entries of d blow up.

transferable: Approximate an SDP bound with quadratic cuts from nonuniform diagonal perturbations, separated by barrier coordinate minimization with closed-form steps and Sherman-Morrison updates (pp. 12, 15-17).
Use the equality constraints only inside the separation problem (alpha*A'A), never inside the cut, to keep sparsity and conditioning (pp. 4, 12).
Regularize a separation SDP with rho*d'd so that its optimum is attained; when |d| exceeds 10 times the shift, raise rho and restart (pp. 15-17).
Run the expensive relaxation once at the root, then pass a multiplier-weighted root perturbation, and each parent's perturbation, down the tree (pp. 18-19).
Measure a root bound on a scale between a cheap reference and the target SDP: (muSDP - muQCP)/(muSDP - muQP) x 100 (p. 21).

Ablation reporting: keep instances where the feature is active and that are not trivial, analyse solved and unsolved instances apart with a 10% similarity band, and use shifted geometric means with shifts of 1 and 10 (pp. 21-23).
coauthors: Carlos J. Nohra (first author; Carnegie Mellon, Department of Chemical Engineering), Arvind U. Raghunathan (Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories)

quotes.text: First, the convex QCP relaxations of the form (33) are at least an order of magnitude more expensive than the QP relaxations of the form (58).

For these instances, the relaxations proposed in this paper provide tighter lower bounds, but the increased computational cost associated with the construction and solution of these relaxations leads to some degradation in performance.
